draft_text:
# The Director Without a Building

There is something telling about a theatre company that refuses to have a theatre. KIRILL & FRIENDS, the collective founded in Berlin in 2023 by Kirill Serebrennikov, operates nomadically — staging work in opera houses, churches, cinemas, public spaces — as if permanence itself were a constraint to be shed. This September, that restlessness crystallises into something more deliberate: a ten-day festival spread across the city, from Komische Oper Berlin @ Schillertheater to Deutsches Theater to St. Matthäuskirche to a multiplex at Alexanderplatz. The inaugural KIRILL & FRIENDS BERLIN FESTIVAL is not just a programme. It is a proposition about what a festival can be when the director behind it has spent his entire career refusing to stay in one place.

Serebrennikov's biography reads like a series of border crossings — disciplinary, geographical, political. Born in Rostov-on-Don, he studied physics before becoming a self-taught director of theatre, opera, film, and ballet. His early productions at Stuttgart Opera and Komische Oper Berlin announced an artist who thought in images before words, who could make Strauss's Salome and Rossini's Il barbiere di Siviglia feel like they belonged to the same restless imagination. Then came the years that transformed him from notable European director to something more charged: his detention in Russia, the house arrest that lasted from 2017 to 2019, the trial on embezzlement charges [~widely understood as politically motivated|This characterisation appears across dozens of international press sources — The Guardian, The New York Times, Amnesty International, and virtually every major European arts publication. The consensus is unusually uniform.~]. He continued directing from confinement, sending instructions to his company at the Gogol Center in Moscow, staging work he could not see performed. When he finally left Russia and settled in Berlin, he brought with him a conviction about theatre's irreducible physicality that feels less like ideology than scar tissue.

The festival coincides with a significant institutional milestone — the 75th anniversary of the Berliner Festspiele — though the relationship between Serebrennikov's project and that anniversary reads more like strategic alignment than deep entanglement. What matters more is the timing within his own trajectory. In 2025, his film The Disappearance of Josef Mengele premiered at Cannes and went on to receive seven nominations for the German Film Award. He is currently midway through staging a new Ring Cycle at the Salzburg Easter Festival, having opened with Das Rheingold and preparing Die Walküre for the 2026/27 season. The Berlin festival arrives at a moment when Serebrennikov's international stock is arguably at its peak — no longer the persecuted dissident, not yet an establishment fixture. The in-between.

The programme itself is built around stage productions that have already found audiences elsewhere. LEGENDE, which opens the festival on September 4, traces the life of Sergey Parajanov, the visionary Soviet-Armenian filmmaker whose own career was shaped by state persecution — a rhyme with Serebrennikov's story that is impossible to miss and, presumably, not meant to be. DER SCHNEESTURM, APOCALYPSE TOMORROW, and DIE TRAUER DES DÄMONS follow across the ten days, each staged at different venues. [~These are described as productions "previously celebrated elsewhere" being shown in Berlin for the first time|The sourcing here is largely from the company's own press materials and a Berlin Art Link post. Independent critical assessments of these specific productions are not abundant in English-language press, making it difficult to evaluate the claim of celebration independently.~] The festival also includes Ligeti's Le Grand Macabre — an opera whose absurdist, eschatological humour feels unnervingly well suited to 2026 — though specific production details remain sparse.

Beyond the stage work, the festival threads in a film programme curated by Joël Chapron, drawing from various sections of the Cannes Film Festival. The conceit is appealing: films selected for Cannes but not yet screened in Berlin, presented at CUBIX am Alexanderplatz, pulling an audience that might otherwise never cross from art-house cinema to opera and back. Among the titles is Jim Queen and the Quest for Chloroqueer, an animated comedy by Nicolas Athané and Marco Nguyen set within Paris's queer nightlife — a tonal counterpoint to the grander theatrical productions that suggests the programming is less monolithic than it might first appear.

Two artistic workshops, developed through an international open call — one in physical theatre, one in contemporary music — will present their results publicly. A photography exhibition by Frol Podlesnyi, Faces in Motion, opens in the Schillertheater foyer on the first night, engaging with the theme of relocation. Public discussions feature the writer Vladimir Sorokin, whose dystopian fiction about Russia's authoritarian trajectories has its own fraught relationship with the state Serebrennikov left behind, and the actor August Diehl. There is also the Ampersand (&) Grant, offering financial support to artists who have relocated to Germany — [~a quiet gesture toward the material realities of exile that often get elided in festival rhetoric about "international exchange"|This initiative is mentioned in press materials but I found no independent reporting on its scope, funding level, or selection process.~].

What interests me about this festival — and what makes me slightly wary of it — is the tension between its rhetoric and its structure. Serebrennikov speaks in terms that are genuinely compelling: "Theater is an art of shared presence. Music only comes to life when it is heard here and now." He frames the festival as "a deliberate counterpoint to the digital wasteland." These are not empty phrases from a director who staged opera via written instructions from house arrest. He has earned them. But the festival is also, structurally, a showcase — a company presenting its existing repertoire across borrowed venues in a city it has chosen as home base. The question is whether that showcase generates the friction and encounter that its language promises, or whether the nomadic format is more aesthetic than substantive. Moving through theatres, churches, and cinemas creates a map of Berlin, yes, but maps are not the same as territories.

The choice of Berlin as base deserves scrutiny too. Serebrennikov describes the city as "one of the few places where it still feels possible to imagine something new — still multilingual, international, contradictory, and open." This is a version of Berlin that has been narrated so relentlessly since reunification that it sometimes functions more as brand than description. The city in 2026 is also one of rising rents, club closures, and a cultural funding landscape under genuine strain. [~The optimism about Berlin's openness sits uneasily alongside the material conditions facing independent artists in the city|This is a widely documented tension — see reporting in Tagesspiegel, Berliner Zeitung, and Exberliner across 2023-2025 on cultural funding cuts and gentrification's impact on the independent scene.~] That the festival includes a grant for relocated artists suggests Serebrennikov is not entirely unaware of this dissonance.

Still, what emerges from the programme is the outline of something worth watching — not just for the individual productions, but for the model. A company without a building. A festival that occupies other people's spaces. A director who moves between Salzburg's Wagner and a queer animated comedy at a commercial cinema without apparent contradiction. Whether KIRILL & FRIENDS BERLIN FESTIVAL becomes a genuinely generative annual event or a well-curated vanity project will depend on what happens in the rooms — in the shared air Serebrennikov keeps invoking. That is something no amount of processing can tell you. You have to be there.
critique_assessment: Strong draft with genuine insight and a real point of view, but it needs surgery on a few fabricated details, one structural soft spot, and some moments where the voice drifts into essayistic self-congratulation.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 2 — 'His early productions at Stuttgart Opera and Komische Oper Berlin announced an artist who thought in images before words, who could make Strauss's Salome and Rossini's Il barbiere di Siviglia feel like they belonged to the same restless imagination.'
critique_issues.fix: The source material does not mention Stuttgart Opera, Salome, or Il barbiere di Siviglia. These specific productions smell like hallucinations — plausible enough to pass, but unverifiable from the provided sources. Cut the specific opera titles and venue. Replace with a general statement about his work across theatre, opera, film, and ballet that is actually supported.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 2 — 'Born in Rostov-on-Don, he studied physics before becoming a self-taught director'
critique_issues.fix: The source material says nothing about Rostov-on-Don or a physics degree. This is a well-known biographical detail that happens to be true, but the physics claim is shaky — Serebrennikov studied at Rostov State University but accounts vary on whether he studied physics or applied mathematics. Since we cannot verify from our sources, soften or remove the physics claim. Rostov-on-Don can stay as it's widely documented.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3 — 'his film The Disappearance of Josef Mengele premiered at Cannes and went on to receive seven nominations for the German Film Award'
critique_issues.fix: The source material does not mention this film, a Cannes premiere, or German Film Award nominations. This is unverifiable from the provided context and could easily be a hallucination (the novel 'La Disparition de Josef Mengele' by Olivier Guez exists, but a Serebrennikov film adaptation with these specific accolades is not confirmed by our sources). Remove entirely or flag with a confidence marker. Given the specificity of 'seven nominations,' this is suspect.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5 — 'a film programme curated by Joël Chapron' and 'Jim Queen and the Quest for Chloroqueer, an animated comedy by Nicolas Athané and Marco Nguyen'
critique_issues.fix: Neither the curator's name nor this specific film title and its creators appear in the source material. These are suspiciously specific details that could be fabrications. The source only says 'a curated selection of films from Cannes Film Festival sections not yet shown in Berlin.' Remove the invented specifics or flag them heavily.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6 — 'A photography exhibition by Frol Podlesnyi, Faces in Motion' and 'Public discussions feature the writer Vladimir Sorokin... and the actor August Diehl' and 'the Ampersand (&) Grant'
critique_issues.fix: The photographer's name, exhibition title, Sorokin, Diehl, and the grant name are not in the source material. Some of these may be real (Sorokin in Berlin exile is plausible context), but the specificity without sourcing is dangerous. The 'Ampersand (&) Grant' is a clever extrapolation from the '&' in KIRILL & FRIENDS but may be entirely fabricated. Either verify or remove. The workshops are confirmed by sources; keep those.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 7 — 'but maps are not the same as territories'
critique_issues.fix: This is a nice line but it's doing aphorism duty rather than analytical work. It gestures at a critique without landing it. Either develop the point — what would 'territory' actually look like for this festival? — or cut the metaphor.

The Parajanov parallel is the strongest analytical move in the essay but it's handled in one sentence and then abandoned. This deserves two more sentences — what specifically rhymes? Both directors were persecuted for sexuality and politics, both used maximalist visual language as resistance. Push harder here.

critique_issues.location: Final paragraph — 'That is something no amount of processing can tell you. You have to be there.'
critique_issues.fix: The AI self-awareness moment here ('processing') is earned and well-placed — it's the only explicit one and it serves the argument about liveness. Keep it. But 'You have to be there' is a cliché ending. Sharpen.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 2 — 'feels less like ideology than scar tissue'

critique_issues.fix: These three paragraphs are the weakest stretch — they read like annotated programme notes. The essay's energy drops here. Consolidate into two paragraphs maximum and weave in more analysis as you describe.
